title: Causal Feature Learning via Generalized Rayleigh Quotients
claim: Combining two complementary properties, temporal dynamics and invariance, in one unified method covers both axes where each alone is incomplete.
layout: 2x2 quadrant grid, axes labeled, arrows converge on top-right combined method box
description: A 2x2 quadrant diagram with a y-axis labeled 'Enforces Invariance' and an x-axis labeled 'Captures Temporal Dynamics'. The top-left green quadrant holds a 'Causal Invariance' box with a checkmark hexagon. Below it is a small sketch of causal graphs (C→Y, S→Y) before and after a red dashed 'Distribution shift' arrow. The bottom-right blue quadrant holds a 'Temporal Causality' box with a clock icon. Below it is a chain X_{t-2}→X_{t-1}→X_t, with X_t in red. The top-right yellow quadrant holds the 'Causal Feature Learning (CFL)' box with a gears icon. A green arrow from the invariance box and a blue arrow from the temporal box both point into it. The bottom-left gray quadrant says 'Solve Generalized Eigenproblem', with an atom icon. The eye goes first to the colored CFL box at top right.
caption: Two complementary aspects of causal features. (a) Temporal causality: time-lagged covariances encode how past variables help predict current states. (b) Causal invariance: causal mechanisms are expected to be stable across environments. CFL extracts features capturing both properties.
abstract: Extracting causally meaningful features from time-series data is fundamental for robust machine learning under distribution shifts. In process monitoring, existing methods struggle to maintain detection performance when operating conditions change. Current approaches capture either temporal causal relationships or cross-environment invariance, but not both simultaneously. We propose Causal Feature Learning (CFL), a unified framework that jointly optimizes for temporal relevance and environment mean invariance. CFL formulates feature extraction as a generalized Rayleigh-quotient problem, maximizing correlation with target variables while penalizing sensitivity to environment-dependent mean shifts. Theoretical analysis establishes conditions under which CFL identifies a mean-invariant predictive subspace. Experiments on the Tennessee Eastman Process demonstrate that CFL achieves 93.69\% average fault detection rate, outperforming 15 baseline methods and validating the benefit of jointly capturing both aspects of causality.
